# Conti Ransomware Leaks and Public Attribution Record

## Executive assessment

The supplied public record supports a coherent description of Conti as a commercially organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation that combined internally developed malware, specialized personnel, affiliates, and a double-extortion business model. The strongest evidence for this characterization comes from the leaked internal chats summarized by Rapid7 and the Center for Internet Security (CIS). Those sources describe recruitment, salary discussions, departmental specialization, malware testing, procurement of security tools, and reliance on outside parties for functions such as initial access and spamming. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The record also shows that the February 2022 leaks exposed operational, financial, technical, and organizational information. Rapid7 reported that the leak contained approximately 14 megabytes of chat logs across 393 JSON files, as well as screenshots, discussions of exploits and development processes, and credentials that the researchers expressly warned readers not to use. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)) The leak therefore provided unusually direct evidence of cybercrime commercialization, although some messages were encrypted and the identity of the leaker was not established.

The U.S. Rewards for Justice page presents Conti—also called Wizard Spider—as a Russian government-linked RaaS group and identifies five online aliases—“Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis”—as malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti. This is an official government attribution and reward statement, but its wording is important: the page says the actors are “believed to be linked,” not that it publicly proves a specific legal identity for each alias. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.-a](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The Department of Justice record separately identifies Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko as defendants in Conti-related federal cases. However, the supplied DOJ page does not map those defendants to the five aliases listed by Rewards for Justice. It describes charges and procedural developments, while emphasizing that defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court. ([U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, n.d.](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)) Accordingly, the evidence supports a relationship between the defendants and alleged Conti activity as reflected in the charging records, but it does not support assigning any particular alias to any particular defendant.

## Source and evidentiary framework

For clarity, this report assigns the following source identifiers to the supplied materials:

| Source ID | Source | Evidentiary role |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Rewards for Justice, “Conti” | Official U.S. government attribution, alias list, threat description, reward notice |
| S2 | Rapid7, “Conti Ransomware Group Internal Chats Leaked Over Russia-Ukraine Conflict” | Technical and organizational analysis of leaked chats |
| S3 | Center for Internet Security, “The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization” | Analysis of Conti’s RaaS structure and commercialization |
| S4 | U.S. Attorney’s Office, Middle District of Tennessee, “Conti Ransomware” | Federal defendant and case information, charges, plea and proceeding records |

The sources do not all make the same type of assertion. S1 is an official government reward announcement and attribution assessment. S2 is a private-sector threat-intelligence analysis based partly on leaked material. S3 is a nonprofit cybersecurity analysis that incorporates the Conti leaks and an MS-ISAC perspective. S4 is an official law-enforcement case page, but it records allegations and procedural events rather than final adjudications for every defendant.

## How public sources describe Conti as an RaaS operation

### Double extortion and monetization

The supplied sources describe Conti as using a double-extortion model. Operators allegedly stole victims’ files and encrypted servers and workstations, then demanded payment. If a victim refused, the stolen information could be sold or published on a site controlled by the actors. Rewards for Justice states that ransom demands varied considerably and could reach $25 million. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.-a](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The RaaS model separated malware development and administration from at least some intrusion activity. CIS explains that RaaS operators lease or provide malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers, commonly using a revenue split described in the article as approximately 70–30. CIS also describes initial access brokers as an important part of this ecosystem because they can sell already established access to victim environments. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

This division of labor increased operational scale. Instead of requiring the core group to perform every intrusion, affiliates or access brokers could supply access, while the central organization focused on software development, support, negotiation, and revenue management. CIS’s conclusion is that commercialization enabled cybercriminals to increase the number of potential victims and to reinvest income into the malware operation. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

### Malware and associated tools

Rewards for Justice associates Conti with the Conti ransomware-as-a-service application and lists Wizard Spider, TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader as associated cyberthreat organizations or applications. The page does not state that every listed tool was developed by Conti; rather, it presents them as associated with the threat activity. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.-a](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

Rapid7 reports that Conti used phishing to establish access, discussed malicious documents and delivery logistics, and tested its malware against endpoint-detection products to improve its ability to avoid detection. The same analysis identifies several vulnerabilities associated with Conti activity, including MS17-010-related vulnerabilities, ZeroLogon, PrintNightmare, Log4Shell, and ProxyShell/ProxyLogon vulnerabilities. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The use of Cobalt Strike is especially relevant to the commercialization account. CIS reports that the leaked material indicated Conti allocated $60,000 to obtain a valid Cobalt Strike license and spent several thousand dollars monthly on security and antivirus software for testing. These details portray an organization investing in both offensive tooling and quality assurance rather than operating as a loose collection of opportunistic criminals. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

## What the leaks exposed

### Organizational specialization

The leaks reportedly revealed a structure resembling a technology company. CIS describes internal units or job categories including “Coders,” “Testers,” “Administrators,” “Reverse Engineers,” and “Penetration Testers/Hackers.” Spamming functions were reportedly outsourced. Each business unit had a budget, although funds could be borrowed between units. CIS further reports that an insider estimated the group employed more than 60 people in July 2021, principally coders and testers. ([Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

Rapid7 similarly describes recruitment processes, coding exercises, salary negotiations, product status discussions, and ordinary workplace communications. The reported interview process resembled a conventional technical hiring process, demonstrating that the group attempted to recruit and manage individuals according to specialized skills. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

### Development, testing, and adaptation

The communications exposed efforts to improve the ransomware product. Rapid7 reports discussions about encryption of very large files, endpoint-detection evasion, target-specific features, malicious document delivery, and compatibility with newer operating systems. CIS reports that reverse engineers were redirected toward Windows 11 in July 2021. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

The practical implication is that Conti’s “product” was treated as an iterative software platform. The group sought to test, update, and adapt its malware to defensive technologies and operating-system changes. This is a supported assessment of operational behavior, not proof that every planned feature was successfully implemented.

### Infrastructure and financial information

Rapid7 states that the leak included screenshots of a Conti control panel showing compromised hosts, operating systems, antivirus products, user rights, and other information about infected assets. The leak also reportedly exposed command-and-control and storage-server access information, usernames, and passwords. Rapid7 did not access the remote systems and warned against doing so. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

Rapid7 further reported that leaked financial information identified a primary Bitcoin address containing more than $2 billion as of February 28, 2022. Because the supplied article characterizes this as information revealed by the chats and does not provide an independent blockchain-verification methodology in the excerpt, the figure should be treated as a reported leak-derived estimate rather than an independently established balance. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

### Political conflict and operational disruption

The leak followed Conti’s public expression of support for the Russian government after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Rapid7 reports that some members sided with Ukraine, creating internal conflict, and that a subsequent message revised the group’s position by condemning the war and threatening retaliation only if Russian critical infrastructure were targeted. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

Rapid7 assessed that Conti’s infrastructure takedowns after the disclosure did not immediately eliminate the threat. Its researchers observed a resumption of normal operations by March 9, 2022. CIS later reported that the larger Conti platform shut down and fragmented into smaller units in 2022, with the data-leak and negotiation infrastructure subsequently ceasing operation. These accounts are not necessarily inconsistent: the first concerns short-term operational resilience after the leak, while the second describes later dismantling and fragmentation. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/); [Center for Internet Security, n.d.](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization))

## Public attribution and law-enforcement record

### Government attribution and aliases

Rewards for Justice offers up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of persons who, while acting at the direction or control of a foreign government, participate in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The page identifies five aliases—“Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis”—as actors believed to be linked to Conti. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.-a](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

The same page characterizes Conti/Wizard Spider as Russian government-linked and says Conti targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. It reports more than 1,000 ransomware operations against U.S. and international critical infrastructure and more than 400 victimized organizations worldwide, including more than 290 in the United States. These are figures presented by Rewards for Justice; the supplied material does not provide an independent methodology or case-by-case victim list, so they should be attributed to the government page rather than treated as independently verified totals. ([U.S. Department of State, n.d.-a](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/))

### Federal defendants and procedural status

The DOJ page identifies two federal case numbers and five defendants. Case 3:23-CR-00092 names Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov. Case 3:23-CR-00088 names Oleksii Lytvynenko. ([U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, n.d.](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

According to the page, the four defendants in the first case were charged in September 2023 with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Lytvynenko was charged in November 2025 with conspiracy to deploy Conti, a ransomware variant that infected computers and networks and encrypted data. The page states that Lytvynenko entered a guilty plea to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, on June 10, 2026, pursuant to a plea agreement. ([U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee, n.d.](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2))

The supplied DOJ record does not establish that all five defendants were convicted of all described conduct, nor does it identify the aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” or “Dandis” as belonging to any named defendant. That distinction is essential. The law-enforcement record establishes named defendants, charges, and one reported guilty plea; Rewards for Justice establishes an official alias-based attribution request; the supplied evidence does not bridge those two sets of identities.

## Contradictions, limitations, and confidence assessment

The evidence is strongest on Conti’s organizational model and operational practices, because Rapid7 and CIS both independently describe specialization, recruitment, testing, outsourcing, and commercialization. Confidence is also high that U.S. authorities publicly associate Conti with the five listed aliases and that federal prosecutors brought Conti-related charges against the named defendants.

Confidence is lower for specific financial figures, the exact relationship between Conti and Russian state actors, and the identity of the individuals behind the aliases. Rewards for Justice uses the term “Russian government-linked,” while Rapid7 reports that one leaked conversation indicated FSB involvement in part of Conti’s funding and interest in information concerning Bellingcat and Alexei Navalny. Rapid7 presents this as an indication from a conversation, not as a judicially established finding. ([Rapid7, 2022](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/))

The principal conclusion is therefore that the public record supports a commercially structured and highly capable RaaS operation, exposed in unusual detail by the 2022 leaks, and later addressed through official attribution and criminal proceedings. It does not support a complete identity-resolution chart connecting every alias, leak username, and defendant.

## Structured findings

| Question | Answer | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Was Conti described as RaaS? | Yes. The sources describe malware developers, affiliates, revenue sharing, outsourced access, and double extortion. | High |
| What did the leaks reveal? | Specialized departments, recruitment, budgets, testing, development priorities, infrastructure, credentials, and financial information. | High, subject to leak limitations |
| Did the leaks prove Conti’s exact membership? | No. They exposed usernames and at least one alleged developer, but the leaker’s identity and complete membership were not established. | High |
| Were aliases publicly linked to Conti? | Yes, Rewards for Justice lists five aliases as believed to be linked to Conti. | High as an official assessment |
| Were aliases mapped to DOJ defendants? | Not in the supplied sources. | High |
| Were defendants convicted? | The supplied record reports charges against several defendants and a guilty plea by Lytvynenko to one count, but not final adjudications for all defendants. | High |

## References

Center for Internet Security. (n.d.). *The Conti leaks: A case of cybercrime’s commercialization*. CIS. [https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization)

Rapid7. (2022, March 1). *Conti ransomware group internal chats leaked over Russia-Ukraine conflict*. Rapid7. [https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/)

U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Middle District of Tennessee. (n.d.). *Conti ransomware*. U.S. Department of Justice. [https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2)

U.S. Department of State. (n.d.-a). *Conti*. Rewards for Justice. [https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/)
